code.title: Entire retention loop (review schedule, strength, completion flags, pre-test) lives only in localStorage; the one server write fails silently
code.fix: Persist completion, review schedule and strength server-side keyed by user_id (a small user_section_state table: completed_at, review_interval_idx, next_due, reviews, quiz_accuracy, pretest_score, pretest_questions). Fix or delete /api/learn-mode/progress: either change last_result to TEXT or stop writing strings; check the upsert error and return 500 so the failure is visible. Hydrate localStorage from the server on login as a cache, not the source of truth.
code.impact: A student who completes a topic on their school laptop and opens Revvy on their phone (or in incognito, or after Safari's 7-day ITP storage eviction, or after clearing site data) has: no completion dot in the sidebar, no strength bar, no scheduled reviews, no pre-test record, and the section re-opens at the DB-saved step with the pre-test gate suppressed only because isResuming is true. The 1/3/7/14-day spaced review promise is broken for anyone who is not on the exact same browser profile every time. Logged-in status changes nothing.
code.evidence: app/api/learn-mode/state/route.js:78-101 reads existing row before upsert so a partial write can't blank other fields; lib/section-state.js:29-40 migrates legacy revvy_complete_/revvy_pretest_ keys on first read; saveSectionState (section-state.js:82-99) writes local first and no-ops safely on 401 signed-out; GET returns {state:{},signedIn:false} when signed out (curl-verified) and {unavailable:true} rather than 500 when the table errors (route.js:58-64)

code.title: Nothing ever brings a student back for a due review; the only 'review due' banner is hidden on the screens a returning student actually lands on
code.fix: Surface due learn-mode reviews on HomeScreen and on the CompletionScreen itself ('Your review of this topic is due tomorrow at ...'). Once the schedule is server-side, add a daily email/push digest of due reviews. Also render the banner above the pre-test gate and completion screen, not just the step view.
code.impact: Day 1 after completing 'introductory-concepts', a student re-opens the app. Every section change lands on the Learn tab; if they open the section they finished, they see the Completion screen (no banner). If they open a new section they first hit the pre-test gate (no banner). Only once they are inside the step view of an unfinished section do they see '1 review due'. Nobody outside the app is told; the review exists only if the student stumbles into it.

code.title: Explain It Back always reads 0/1 with an empty bar on every completion screen because the attempt callback is never wired
code.fix: Pass onExplainAttempt into ExplainItBackUpgraded and call it on submit (or on graded result for premium). Hide the Explain row when total is 0, and hide the 20% weight label unless a composite score is actually computed and shown.
code.impact: Every student who answers at least one quiz or recall sees a 'Score Breakdown' in which 'Explain It Back 0/1' sits with an empty bar and a 20% weight, regardless of whether they wrote three paragraphs and got AI feedback. It reads as 'you failed this' or 'the app is broken'. Free users, who cannot get their explanation graded, are told they scored 0 on a component they were never allowed to complete.
code.evidence: components/LearnModeTab.jsx:83-86 onExplainAttempt wired to both ExplainItBackUpgraded instances (lines 473,515); components/learn-mode/CompletionScreen.jsx:94-101 row hidden when total=0, weight labels removed; components/learn-mode/ExplainItBackUpgraded.jsx:16-22 free users counted via onBlur (line 81), premium via handleGrade (line 40)

code.title: Strength meter maths guarantee a completed topic is amber on the completion screen, red within 2 days, ~11% after a week
code.fix: Rebase the model: completion should land at a clearly positive value (e.g. 70-80) and decay should follow the scheduled interval (strength hits the 'review' threshold roughly when the review is due, not two days in). Feed inline quiz correctness, post-test and quick-fire results into quizAccuracy. Show 'Review due in N days' rather than a decaying percentage on the completion screen. Do not show a decaying bar in the sidebar next to a completion dot.
code.impact: The first thing under 'Topic complete' is an amber bar saying '35% strength'. Coming back tomorrow it is 30%, then red. A student who completes five topics in a week sees a sidebar full of red slivers next to every green completion dot. The 14-day review interval the app schedules is incompatible with its own meter: by the time the review is due the meter says <10% even after a perfect previous review. Nothing the student does inside Learn Mode (inline quiz, explain-it-back, recalls, quick-fire, post-test) raises the meter except a SpacedReview or MixedReview.
code.evidence: components/Sidebar.jsx:6 the StrengthMeter import is gone and 150-177 renders one status glyph only, so no decaying bar sits beside the completion dot anywhere in the sidebar; the new due state is derived in a mount effect at Sidebar.jsx:29-40 (getStrengthData + nextReviewAt) with an empty Set as initial state, so nothing reads localStorage during render and no hydration mismatch is possible (app/globals.css:417 styles .due; localhost:3001 console clean, no hydration warning). Residuals recorded, not blocking: CompletionScreen.jsx:106 still prints the percentage next to the date (StrengthMeter.jsx:53 renders n% strength - review in N days) rather than the date alone, and inline-quiz correctness still never reaches quizAccuracy (LearnModeTab.jsx:309 calls recordReview with null; only the drill/post-test at CompletionScreen.jsx:44-46 and ReviewMode do), so the sidebar due flag at nextReviewAt can also lead the 1/3/7/14 schedule written at LearnModeTab.jsx:302 by roughly half an interval

code.title: Post-test and Quick Fire results are discarded: they never affect strength, the review schedule, or the server
code.fix: On post-test and drill completion, call recordReview(subjectId, sectionId, score) and (once server-side) update the schedule: a strong post-test could push the first review from 1 day to 3.
code.impact: A student who does the post-test and goes 1/3 -> 3/3 sees 'Perfect score! You've mastered this topic', then the strength meter above it still says 35% and tomorrow's review is still due. Effort in the optional activities has no visible consequence anywhere else in the app.
code.evidence: PostTest.jsx:43-49 and QuickFireDrill.jsx:110-114 each report onScore exactly once via a reportedRef guard; both wired to CompletionScreen.jsx:43-47 handleDrillScore, which calls recordReview() and saveSectionState({quizAccuracy, reviewed}) at lines 45-46, reaching strength.js and the server schedule

code.title: Score Breakdown is component state: it disappears on revisit and double-counts on Retry; weights 50/30/20 label a composite that is never computed
code.fix: Persist per-attempt scores with the completion record; reset scores in onRetry; drop the weight labels or compute and display the composite; require at least 3 quiz answers before the 'needs attention' callout.
code.impact: First time: a breakdown with 'Quiz 0/1 50%' and a warning 'Quiz questions need attention' after a single wrong click. Tomorrow: the same screen with no breakdown at all. After Retry: 'Quiz 1/2' even though they answered the single question right the second time. The percentages imply a mastery score the app never calculates.
code.evidence: components/learn-mode/CompletionScreen.jsx:128-153 gates the weakest-area callout on MIN_ANSWERS=3 and WEAK_BELOW=0.7 (filter on a.s.total >= MIN_ANSWERS at line 141), so one wrong answer out of one can no longer produce a verdict; it now ranks quiz against recall by accuracy and names the worse of the two with the raw count. Persistence and retry reset already stood: LearnModeTab.jsx:99-101 seeds scores from readLocalState, :292 writes them with the completion record, :364-366 resets a fresh zeroed object on Retry; weight labels gone at CompletionScreen.jsx:107-110. code.title: Recall score counts only attempted widgets; dismissing with the x is invisible
code.fix: Report skips to the parent (onComplete(null) or an onSkip prop) and show 'Recall 1 of 10 attempted, 1 correct'; de-duplicate by recall prompt so the spaced re-attempt updates rather than appends.
code.impact: Skip nine reorders, check one: 'Recall 1/1' with a full bar. Do the same fill-in twice: 2/2. The number is technically not false but it does not measure what the label implies.

code.title: Same MCQ bank is reused for pre-test, inline quiz, spaced review (identical 5 forever), quick fire, and the Quiz tab; pre-test reveals the answers first
code.fix: Do not reveal correct answers on the pre-test (score only, or reveal after completion). Partition the bank: reserve questions not used in pre-test/inline for reviews, and re-sample review questions from the section at each interval rather than freezing them at completion. Retire an entry after the 14-day pass or extend to 30/60 days.
code.impact: A section with 8 MCQs: the student sees three of them (with answers revealed) before learning, sees them again inline, again in the post-test, again in quick fire, again in the Quiz tab, and the same 5 every 1, 3, 7, 14, 14, 14... days. 'Improvement' on the post-test mostly measures having seen the green highlight 20 minutes earlier. Reviews become answer-recognition, not retrieval.
code.evidence: CONFIRMED. Both rejected sub-clauses are closed, verified live on dev 3001 at 390px against a served bundle re-read from the page (isDue, the MixedReview write-back and the post-test retry are all present in the delivered chunks, describesOption is not, so no stale JSX). (1) ONE DUE PREDICATE. ReviewMode.jsx:46-48 isDue(entry,now) = !!entry && !entry.retired && entry.nextDue <= now, used by countDueReviews (:52) and getDueReviews (:63) and by nothing else; both forms confirmed in the served bundle, not just the source. Live with two retired overdue entries plus one non-retired overdue entry the banner read '1 review due' and 'Review now' opened the Spaced Review for the non-retired topic (Live Gamma) - count, button and list all agree, and the non-retired due topic is still offered. With ONLY the two retired overdue entries the banner does not render at all: no number, no dead control. NO THIRD ROUTE: revvy_review_schedule is read in exactly three places - ReviewMode.jsx:21, LearnModeTab.jsx:308 (write) and CompletionScreen.jsx:54, and the last is .length for the 'Mixed review (N topics)' CTA, not a due count. HomeScreen/ProgressDashboard overdueCount comes from app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:181-186 over server per-question SM-2 rows and never reads this schedule; lib/spaced-repetition.js is the practice engine's own queue. (2) RETIREMENT IS REVERSIBLE. ReviewMode.jsx:297-321. Live, mixed review scored 0/9 across two retired and one never-retired entry: both retired entries came back retired true->false, currentInterval 5->4, nextDue +30d, lastScore 0; the never-retired entry was byte-identical afterwards, so the guard at :308 (score >= 0.6 || !entry.retired) cannot resurrect a topic that was never retired. Entry stays valid for every other reader: the ...entry spread kept questions, intervals [1,3,7,14,30,60], title, subjectId and optionsShuffled, and reviewsDone is deliberately unchanged so SpacedReview's window (:137) does not jump. A GOOD mixed review does not advance: 9/9 on the same fixture left revvy_review_schedule byte-identical (retired still true, currentInterval 5, nextDue delta 0) while recordReview still fired. QUOTA: with Storage.prototype.setItem made to throw for revvy_review_schedule only, a 0/6 mixed review left the schedule unchanged (1 write blocked, swallowed by the bare catch at :123) but revvy_strength_1_retired-alpha and _live-gamma were both written (reviews 1, quizAccuracy 0) and the result screen rendered with no React error - recordReview at :301 runs inside the loop, saveSchedule at :321 after it, so the strength write cannot be lost to a schedule quota failure. REACHABILITY, residual not blocking: MixedReview has exactly two entry points - the Learn banner (LearnModeTab.jsx:453, gated on dueReviews > 0, so unreachable when everything is retired) and CompletionScreen.jsx:215, gated on completedCount >= 3. Verified live that the second works: with 3 retired topics and nothing due, 'Mixed review (3topics)' appeared on the completion screen and a 0/9 run un-retired all three. But with exactly 2 scheduled topics, both retired, there is no banner and no mixed control anywhere, so for a student with fewer than 3 completed sections retirement is still one-way. Narrow (a topic needs 55+ days of correct reviews to retire) and the student sees an honest zero rather than a wrong number, so not held against the finding. Also still true and pre-existing: saveSchedule's failure is entirely silent to the student. AST sweep over all 34 changed .js/.jsx in 1c98d69^..a11f3e6 clean for TDZ reads, hooks after a conditional return and used-but-unimported identifiers; checker validated by reproducing 163fd01 LearnModeTab.jsx:363 TDZ, 526f4e4 PostTest.jsx:63-64 hooks and 163fd01 PracticeEngine.jsx:347 missing useEffect import. Console over the whole walkthrough: only pre-existing signed-out 401s and umami CSP/CORS noise.

code.fix: Record the skip (e.g. { skipped: true, timestamp }) so the gate is shown once; consider making the pre-test opt-in ('Want to test what you know first?') rather than a gate, and offer the post-test from a fresh sample when no pre-test exists.

code.title: Home 'Mastery', 'Streak', 'This Week' and /progress ignore Learn Mode, Quiz tab and Flashcards tab entirely
code.fix: Define one mastery model that ingests Learn Mode inline quiz/recall results, Quiz tab attempts and Flashcards tab reviews alongside Smart Practice; compute streak from any learning activity (including user_content_progress.updated_at); until then, hide the Mastery/Streak tiles for users with no practice rows rather than showing zeros.

code.evidence: RE-CONFIRMED after the approach changed (bare bracketed letters are no longer rewritten at all; describesOption and the symbolic pre-scan are deleted - grep finds neither anywhere in app/, components/, lib/, scripts/). Independent scanner rerun over all 43 audit/content-sections/*.json, 769 questions, with a FORCED DERANGEMENT oldToNew[i]=(i+1)%n driven through the exported remapOptionLetters: my own raw-char standalone A-F detector, my own bracket-depth counter and my own backwards keyword-list walker, no tokeniser or rule shared with lib/shuffle-options.js. Results: 744 shuffled, 25 declined, 89 explanations changed, 262 letters moved, and 0 references pointing at a different option, 0 duplicated letters, 0 length changes, 0 characters changed outside a single A-F swap, 0 swaps that are not the derangement image. Correct-answer TEXT unchanged for all 769 through shuffleOptions, and the option multiset is preserved in every shuffled question. Stale census over the 744 shuffled: 421 standalone A-F letters, 262 claimed as keyword-list references and all 262 moved, 0 bare-bracketed, 0 bracketed-but-not-alone, 159 loose - and of those 159 ZERO are inside brackets and ZERO are within six words of option/answer/statement, so no missed reference remains. Distribution A4.8/B64.0/C28.5/D2.7 -> A25.6/B24.1/C24.6/D25.7 under the live salt, so the best blind single-letter guess falls from 64.0% to 25.7% against a 25% floor. Non-references still stay: 'Plan B', 'Grade A', 'A rise in income', 'from A to B', 'the options available to a firm', and the documented 'Option A describes area B only' (A moves, the Lorenz area B does not). MY PREVIOUS FOOLING CASE NOW DECLINES: options[2]='Consumer spending rises and firms invest more' with 'raises consumer spending (C) and investment (I)' - hasUnhandledLetterReference true, shuffleOptions returns the identical object. NEW FOOLING CASES AGAINST THE KEYWORD PATH, which is now the only path that rewrites anything - six constructed, six rewrite, none declines. The list continues over separators, joiners and bracketed glosses, so any standalone A-F reached that way is remapped whatever it means: 'Option C, B to D on the diagram, shows the fall in real output.' -> B (a diagram point) becomes C while D does not move; 'The answer C + I + G + (X-M) is the expenditure definition of aggregate demand.' -> the Consumption symbol becomes D, the exact corruption class the bare-bracket rule was deleted to prevent, now reachable through the keyword instead; 'the options B2B, B2C and C2C' -> 'C2B, B2C and C2C' (the letter is not standalone to a human but the tokeniser splits on the digit); 'Options A (a tax rise) and B (a spending cut), C and I are left unchanged.' -> C wrongly moved; 'The options (fiscal, monetary and supply-side) A government may use' -> A moved, because a gloss immediately after the keyword also opens the list; 'Statement A and B, D on the data-response paper' -> D moved. ZERO live instances: of the 262 remapped letters, 31 are reached by list continuation rather than sitting straight after the keyword, and I read all 31 - every one is a genuine 'Options A, C and D' reference. So this is one content edit away, exactly as the bracket rule was, but it is not shipping a defect today. STILL REMAINS, content work the fix itself marks Separately: pick-the-longest scores 70.2% (540/769) because option TEXT is untouched. THE 25 DECLINES, judged: all 25 are forced for the code as it stands, because a bracketed A-F cannot be told from a symbol either way without reading the sentence, and guessing wrong in either direction corrupts. But only 10 are unavoidable in content terms - aggregate-demand q1/q11/q13/q20, macroeconomic-objectives-policies q4/q11/q18, national-income q5/q13 and poverty-inequality q3, where the bracketed letter is the standard IAL expenditure identity C+I+G+(X-M) or the Gini A/(A+B) and cannot be edited away. The other 15 are recoverable: 14 are genuine option references written as bare '(A)' ('TV ads (A), billboards (B)') which shuffle immediately once rewritten as 'Option A' - verified by editing one and re-running - and marketing-mix-strategy q4 is the idiom 'from A to B'. So 10 unavoidable, 15 a judgement call about content effort.

code.title: Any key whose name starts with a-d (Ctrl, Alt, Arrow keys, Backspace, CapsLock) selects an answer
code.fix: Require `e.key.length === 1` before the letter comparison (and ignore events with ctrlKey/metaKey/altKey).
code.impact: A student who presses Ctrl (e.g. Ctrl+Tab to switch tab) or an arrow key to scroll has an answer silently selected and the card moves to phase 1 ('Check answer' lit). If they then press Enter expecting to advance, the wrong answer is checked and recorded into SM-2.
code.evidence: QuestionCard.jsx:32-33 isPrintable=e.key.length===1&&!ctrlKey&&!metaKey&&!altKey rules out ArrowDown/Control/Alt/Backspace/CapsLock (all length>1) and blocks single-char keys held with a modifier

code.title: Confidence is never collected in Smart Practice; Learn Mode's confidence prompt writes to a localStorage key nothing reads
code.fix: Either add a 3-button confidence row to QuestionCard after reveal and pass it to computeNextReview (the lib already supports it), or remove the InlineQuiz confidence prompt until it feeds scheduling. Do not ship a prompt whose data is discarded.
code.impact: Lucky guesses in Smart Practice are scheduled identically to confident knowledge, so a B-guesser (see the bias finding) accumulates 'mastered' (repetitions>=3) cards they cannot actually answer. In Learn Mode the student is interrupted by a 4-second confidence prompt whose answer changes nothing they will ever see, which reads as a pointless widget.

code.title: 'This question will come back' is false within a session; 'RETRIED' stat counts questions that were never retried

code.impact: A student who gets 6 wrong is told six times the question will come back, finishes the 20-question session without seeing any of them again, and then sees 'RETRIED 6' on the summary. The product promises a Leitner-style loop it does not deliver in the moment the student expects it.

code.impact: This is the most direct code-level cause of the 'doesn't cover all topics' complaint: a diligent student is told outright there are no questions for the topic they just studied. They cannot tell the difference between 'you're up to date' and 'the app has no content here'.

code.title: Pre-test questions reappear as the block's inline quiz (~50% of sections) and the post-test is the identical 3 questions in identical order
code.fix: Exclude the union of all blocks' quizIndices from the pre-test pool; for the post-test, sample 3 DIFFERENT questions on the same sub-topics (or at least re-shuffle options) and label it honestly. Also fix the pre-test copy: 'Perfect — your brain is now primed' after 0/3 (PreTest.jsx:135) reads as sarcasm to a nervous student.
code.impact: Half of students see a pre-test question again a few minutes later as the 'Quick quiz' with the answer already revealed, and every student takes a post-test where remembering 'it was B' counts as improvement. The pre/post delta shown on the completion screen is not evidence of learning.
code.evidence: RE-CONFIRMED after the derangement retry landed. PostTest.jsx:65-70 tries salts 'post-test', 'post-test1' ... 'post-test7' until the option order actually differs from the pre-test's. Measured over the whole corpus by replaying what the pre-test stores (shuffleOptions(q,'') - the order StudyApp.jsx:388 hands to PreTest) and then running PostTest's exact loop: 769 questions, 744 shuffled, IDENTICAL REPLAYS 0, down from the 36 I measured before. Max salts used 3; the loop never exhausted its 8. Terminates for a declined question: shuffleOptions returns the same object identity when it declines, PostTest.jsx:68 breaks on 'moved === q', and decline does not depend on the salt, so all 25 declines exit on attempt 1 and are left alone on purpose. Carried userAnswer still points at the same option text: checked every possible pre-test choice on every shuffled question (744 x 4 = 2976 cases) through PostTest.jsx:71-74 - 0 cases where moved.options[at] is not the identical string the student picked. Out-of-range or non-numeric userAnswer falls back to the stored value (indexOf -1 path), so no silent reinterpretation. Two-option question still behaves: synthetic 2-option post-test ran on attempt 1, orders differ, correctIndex moved 1->0 and the correct option TEXT is preserved. RESIDUAL, not live and not blocking: for a 2-option question each salt has a 1/2 chance of the identity order, so the 8-salt loop can exhaust - a synthetic sweep of 744 two-option questions gave 4 identical replays (0.54%, against the 1/256 the loop predicts), and on exhaustion the loop keeps the last attempt, which is a valid question object with a correctly remapped explanation, just the same order. The live corpus has no such question: all 769 have exactly 4 options. The other half of the finding is unchanged from the previous confirmation - PostTest.jsx and PreTest.jsx are the only files in F079's scope touched since it, and the fallback post-test path (PostTest.jsx:34-40) and the pre-test's reserved-question exclusion (PreTest.jsx:17-28) are untouched by 6ce44e1.

code.fix: Content rules for the pipeline: no 'Evaluate/Assess/To what extent' stems in MCQ; max one absolute-word distractor per question; every key must be defensible against the Edexcel IAL definition; use international or neutral contexts (Singapore MAS, HKMA, Bank Negara, generic 'central bank'); one currency convention per subject.

Enforced at scripts/_content-write.mjs:102-107 and scripts/publish-section.mjs:114-124. code.title: React hydration fails on page load: script tags rendered inside React components make the server and client HTML disagree
code.fix: Move the JSON-LD and analytics script tags out of the React component tree. In the App Router, structured data belongs in a route Metadata field or a next/script component with an explicit strategy, not an inline script rendered as a child. Verify with a clean console on a section page.

content.text: Supply and Factors Affecting Supply > what-is-supply > realExample (UK strawberry farmers): Backwards and teaches the wrong concept. UK strawberry retail prices are LOWEST in summer because that is peak season; farmers supply more in summer because of growing conditions (seasonality = a supply SHIFT), not because 'retail prices are highest'. Presented as 'the law of supply in action' (movement along the curve), it is a textbook example of the opposite. Also UK-centric for an international cohort.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/2026-09-11-post-packet-0__business__the-market.json content>what-is-supply>realExample.text now reads 'Ride-hailing drivers ... movement along the supply curve'; law-of-supply/shift confusion removed

content.text: Price Elasticity of Demand (PED) > ped-and-revenue > realExample (UK government tobacco taxation): Claims 'total tax revenue increases each year'. HMRC tobacco duty receipts peaked around 2021-22 (~£10.3bn) and have fallen since (~£8.8bn 2023-24, lower again 2024-25). Also conflates government tax revenue with a firm's total revenue (TR = P x Q), which is the concept being taught; the addictive-good framing is Economics 2.x/market failure territory.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/packet-18-bundle__business__the-market.json:1318-1321 ped-and-revenue realExample is now a generic transport-fare example; the false tobacco-tax-revenue claim is gone

content.text: Demand and Factors Affecting Demand > what-is-demand > realExample (Sony PS5): 'Sony cut the price of the PS5 in several markets to boost sales in 2024. As the price dropped, quantity demanded rose sharply.' Sony's headline 2024 move was a ~19% price RISE in Japan (Sept 2024), followed by rises in Europe/UK/Australia (Apr 2025) and the US (Aug 2025); 2024 saw only short promotional discounts, and PS5 shipments fell year-on-year in FY2024. The example as written is not true and will confuse students who read the news.
content.evidence: audit/snapshots/packet-18-bundle__business__the-market.json:41-44 what-is-demand realExample is now a generic supermarket-cola example; the false Sony PS5 price-cut claim is gone

content.text: Re-align assessment to teaching: either add a block 'Why grow, and what goes wrong' teaching internal/external economies of scale, diseconomies and overtrading (lift from extras.chains[2],[3] and flashcards), or pin quizIndices/practiceIndices per block so PreTest/InlineQuiz only draw from taught items. Right now half the quiz bank and 3/5 practice questions are untaught.

Replace the demergers subsection (off-spec, and its eBay/Skype example is factually wrong: it was a stake sale, not a demerger) with 'Problems of growth: diseconomies of scale and overtrading', which fixes both the spec gap and the incoherent block-2 pairing.

Add an InlineDiagram for block 1: supply chain (raw materials > manufacturer > distributor > retailer > consumer) with arrows showing backward vertical, forward vertical and horizontal integration, matching common_mistakes[1].

Add recall widgets: a fillin on the four integration types (e.g. 'A car maker buying a steel mill is ___ vertical integration; buying a dealership network is ___; buying a rival car maker is ___') and a reorder of the takeover-to-synergy sequence already given as a flow in external-growth-methods.

Swap practice idx 2 (Ansoff) and idx 3 (barriers to entry) for on-spec items, e.g. 'Explain one problem a business may face from rapid growth (4)' and 'Assess the financial risks and rewards to [case firm] of a takeover of [target] (10)', and add a levels-style mark scheme (KAA/Evaluation bands) to the 10- and 20-markers so students can self-mark; de-UK the CMA/MegaRetail references for the international audience.

Growth Decisions > demergers-splitting-up > realExample: States 'eBay demerged Skype in 2009, eventually selling it to Microsoft'. eBay did not demerge Skype (shareholders received no Skype shares); it sold a ~65-70% stake to a Silver Lake-led investor group in 2009, and that group sold Skype to Microsoft in 2011 for $8.5bn. This is a divestment/sale, which contradicts the section's own definition of a demerger two paragraphs earlier.

Growth Decisions > demergers-splitting-up (whole subsection incl. examMatters 'Examiners test whether you can evaluate demergers'): Demergers are an Edexcel Economics (WEC13 3.1.3) topic, not a WBS13 3.2 Business growth bullet. The examMatters claim that IAL Business examiners test demergers is, to my knowledge, unfounded and displaces spec content (diseconomies, overtrading, financial risks/rewards of takeovers) that IS examined.

content.text: q0: Correct answer (index 1) is right, but internal vs external economies of scale are never taught anywhere in content[] (only in flashcards/extras). Because PreTest draws 3 random MCQs and inline quizzes draw from this bank, students are gated/assessed on untaught material.

q2: Answer correct, but diseconomies of scale are only mentioned in passing (one clause in external-growth misconception and staying-small examMatters); never taught as a concept with causes. Untaught material in the assessment bank.
q3: Answer correct and well-explained, but overtrading does not appear anywhere in content[]. It is a named IAL spec bullet (problems arising from growth) so it should be taught, not just quizzed.

q7: Same as index 3: untaught. Also the explanation only justifies the correct answer and one distractor; 'Rapid recruitment of new staff' as a distractor is fine but should be explained as worsening cash outflow.

p2: 'Assess the usefulness of Ansoff's Matrix for a business deciding on its growth strategy' (10 marks) is a 3.1 Business objectives and strategy question, not 3.2 Business growth; Ansoff is never mentioned in this section's content. Also the question is generic ('a business') while a specific gym-chain context is supplied; IAL would phrase it 'Assess the usefulness of Ansoff's Matrix to the gym chain when deciding its growth strategy'. Mark allocation (10, Assess) is correct for IAL Business.

p3: 'Explain two barriers to entry that might prevent new firms from entering a market' (4 marks) is off-topic for 3.2 Business growth (it is Economics / at best 3.5 competitiveness). Nothing in content[] teaches barriers to entry. Should be replaced with an on-spec 4-marker (e.g. 'Explain one reason why a growing business might experience diseconomies of scale' or 'Explain one problem of rapid growth').

Assessment/teaching mismatch: 5 of 10 MCQs (idx 0,2,3,7,8) and 3 of 5 practice questions (idx 0,2,3) test economies of scale, diseconomies, overtrading, Ansoff and barriers to entry, none of which are taught in content[]. With quizIndices/practiceIndices null, the PreTest gate (3 random MCQs) and each block's InlineQuiz/InlinePractice can surface untaught questions, which directly feeds the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Zero recall widgets in either block: Learn Mode has no retrieval practice at all for this section. Obvious candidates: reorder 'takeover process' (identify target > bid premium > regulator review > integration > synergies realised/lost) from external-growth flow; fillin on the four integration types using the supermarket/food-processor/farm/delivery chain.

Zero diagrams: common_mistakes[1] literally tells students to 'draw a simple supply chain diagram in your head' (raw materials > manufacturing > distribution > retail > consumer) to place the two firms. That should be an actual InlineDiagram on block 1 (with backward/forward/horizontal arrows).

2-per-step pairing: with 2 sections per block the whole section is 2 steps. Block 1 pairing (organic + external) is coherent. Block 2 pairs 'Reasons for Staying Small' with 'Demergers', which are unrelated concepts; a student gets one step with two disconnected ideas. Replace demergers with 'Problems of growth: diseconomies and overtrading' so block 2 becomes 'When growth goes wrong / when not to grow'.

Difficulty ramp: the section jumps from definitional prose straight to a 20-mark evaluate with no intermediate teaching of the economic logic (why grow: economies of scale, market power; why it hurts: diseconomies, overtrading). The extras.chains[2] and [3] contain exactly this material, so it exists but is paywalled/hidden from the Learn Mode path.

Takeaways: Block 1 takeaway[3] ('culture clash is the primary reason') overclaims relative to the body. Block 2 takeaway[3] tells students to evaluate demergers from stakeholder perspectives, which trains for a question type that WBS13 is unlikely to set.

Misconceptions: organic-growth ('always safest') and staying-small ('means the firm failed') are genuine student errors. external-growth ('bigger is always better') is plausible. demergers ('demergers mean the firm failed') is filler given the topic itself is off-spec.
Notes[] only has 3 entries (Organic, External, Staying Small) so the Notes tab and Learn Mode disagree on scope (notes omit demergers), another sign the demerger subsection was bolted on.

3.2.1 Growth (a) Objectives of growth: economies of scale (internal and external, with named types: purchasing, technical, managerial, financial, marketing), increased market power over customers and suppliers, increased market share and brand recognition, increased profitability. Not taught; only in flashcards/extras and quizzed.

Financial Ratios > liquidity-gearing-ratios > realExample: Claims Tesla's ROCE went 'from negative figures in 2019 to over 25% by 2023'. Tesla's ROCE peaked around 25% in FY2022 (operating income ~$13.7bn on ~$55bn capital employed); in FY2023 operating income fell to ~$8.9bn on ~$77bn capital employed, roughly 11-12%, after aggressive price cuts. The 2023 date makes the claim wrong, and the example is also about ROCE (profitability) but sits in the liquidity/gearing section, which has no liquidity or gearing example at all.

Core Competencies > vrio-framework > examMatters: 'Examiners reward structured VRIO analysis' — VRIO is not in the Edexcel IAL Business specification or mark schemes (the spec language in 3.1.2 is 'achieving competitive advantage through distinctive capabilities'). A student gets analysis credit for any coherent chain, but telling them examiners specifically reward VRIO misrepresents how IAL papers mark.

(20 marks) — the question is generic and does not reference the smartphone context it is given; IAL 20-markers are anchored ('Evaluate whether [the manufacturer] should...'). Across all five questions there is zero practice on ratio calculation/interpretation, financial statements or HR measures — none of the section's actual spec content is examined in writing.

Spec mismatch is structural, not cosmetic: content[] = Block 1 'Financial Ratios' (mostly Unit 2 recap plus ROCE/gearing) + Block 2 'Core Competencies' (VRIO, not Edexcel). The IAL 3.5 content — interpretation of the income statement and statement of financial position, stakeholder interest, HR measures and HR strategies — has no block at all.

Quiz and practice banks are inverted relative to the content: all 10 MCQs are ratios/HR (0 on Block 2's VRIO/competencies), while all 5 practice questions are strategy frameworks (0 on Block 1's ratios). Whatever the InlineQuiz picks for the Core Competencies step cannot match what was just taught.
Blocks carry no quizIndices, practiceIndices or diagramRef keys, so inline quiz/practice selection for each step is unanchored to the block content.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin across 4 subsections): the only retrieval practice between pre-test and post-test is the single inline MCQ per block. Formula-heavy content is the ideal case for fillin recalls (e.g. ROCE = operating profit ÷ ___ × 100) and none exist.

Only 2 steps in total; each step packs two dense sections (7 paragraphs/flows) plus inline quiz, practice, Explain-It-Back and takeaway. Heavy per-step load with no ramp: step 1 is formulas, step 2 is abstract strategy theory, with no bridge explaining why ratios 'assess competitiveness' (notes[0] has the link — 'higher ROCE than rivals attracts investment' — but the Learn content does not).
0 diagrams. Not fatal for ratios, but a VRIO decision funnel or a 'gearing amplifies returns/losses' bar comparison would replace two of the text flows.

The liquidity-gearing section's realExample is about ROCE; its examMatters is about limitations of ratios in general. The section therefore has no gearing/liquidity example and no gearing-specific exam advice (e.g. link gearing to interest-rate rises or to financing a takeover — classic IAL Unit 3 evaluation).

Numbering '3.3.5' does not match the IAL spec, where assessing competitiveness is 3.5 (3.5.1-3.5.3); 3.3 is decision-making techniques. Unsure whether the app uses its own outline, but students cross-referencing the spec will be confused.

content.text: Trade Blocs > trade-creation-vs-diversion > realExample: Claims 'Post-Brexit, UK fisheries lost tariff-free access to the EU single market' and calls the EU switching to Norwegian salmon 'trade diversion ... (Norway has an EEA arrangement)'. Under the EU-UK TCA (2021) UK-origin goods including Scottish salmon are tariff-free and quota-free; what changed is non-tariff barriers (customs declarations, export health certificates). Norway's EEA membership excludes fisheries and Norwegian salmon actually pays an EU tariff, so this is not trade diversion caused by a CET at all. Scottish salmon exports to France/EU hit records in 2023, so the 'increasingly switch' claim is also unsupported. The example teaches the concept wrongly.

Replace the Hofstede section with a spec-aligned 'Language, translation, branding and social media' section using verified examples (drop the Chevrolet Nova myth from flashcards[11]/common_mistakes[4]; replace the KFC anecdote), and demote Hofstede to the existing extras chain.

Fix quiz index 2 (sachets: accept Product or rewrite the stem to ask about 'price point', e.g. 'selling at a lower unit price to match low incomes') and rewrite quiz index 7's absurd distractors; retire the white-colour trivia item (index 5).

Add recall widgets and one diagram: a fillin on the three approach names (template 'A ___ approach applies the home-market mix abroad; a ___ approach adapts fully per country; a ___ approach mixes the two'), a reorder on the glocalisation decision process (audit culture → decide which 4Ps to standardise vs adapt → test locally → launch), and a standardisation–adaptation spectrum or Ansoff grid diagram.

Convert practice guidance into IAL levels mark schemes (K/A/An/E with level descriptors), change practice[3] to 'Explain one way...' (4 marks), fix the product-development conflation in its guidance, and repair the practice[4] India context so it does not contradict the section's own McDonald's example.

content[1] 'Cultural Influences on Global Marketing' > hofstede-dimensions > realExample: The KFC 'eat your fingers off' story is an unverified marketing legend (hedged with 'reportedly' but then built on as fact). More importantly it is presented as the Hofstede example yet applies no Hofstede dimension; it invokes 'high-context' (Edward Hall's framework, not Hofstede's) and asserts a translation error was inappropriate 'in a collectivist culture', which is a non-sequitur. Students copying this into an exam would show confused theory.

q2: Two options are defensible. Sachets are a packaging/size change (Product) that enables a lower price point (Price); Edexcel textbooks describe sachet strategies under product adaptation as often as under pricing. The explanation itself says 'by selling smaller quantities' (a product change). correctIndex=1 (Price) will be marked wrong for a student who reasonably answers Product.

Zero recall exercises (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with 2 blocks of 2 sections each, Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps, each of which is read, read, one MCQ, one written question, explain-it-back, takeaway. No spaced/immediate recall widgets fire at all.

Quiz/content mismatch: 5 of 10 MCQs (indices 1,3,4,6,8) examine terms never taught in content[] (ethnocentric/polycentric/geocentric, Ansoff, Porter, niche markets). The PreTest draws 3 random items from this bank, so roughly half of pretests will contain untaught material, which directly feeds the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis.

Block 1 'Standardisation vs Adaptation' has sections on standardisation and glocalisation only; the spec's three named approaches (domestic/ethnocentric, mixed/geocentric, international/polycentric) are the examinable vocabulary and are absent, while takeaway[1] summarises an 'Adaptation' section that does not exist.

Block 2 spends one of two sections on Hofstede (off-spec) and compresses six spec bullets (language, unintended meanings, translations, branding/promotion, social media, different tastes) into one section; social media is never mentioned anywhere in content[].

Section is numbered 4.3.3 and titled 'Global Marketing', but in the IAL WBS14 spec 4.3 is the topic ('Global marketing') with 4.3.1 Marketing, 4.3.2 Niche markets, 4.3.3 Cultural/social factors. The content spans 4.3.1 and 4.3.3 but the numbering suggests only the latter; niche markets (4.3.2) exist only in flashcards/quiz/practice/extras.

Misconceptions: global-standardisation ('always cheaper') and cultural-mistakes-brand-impact ('only translations') are genuine student errors. glocalisation's misconception ('simple middle ground') is filler: it is an assertion that glocalisation is 'harder, not easier' rather than a correction of something students actually write. hofstede-dimensions' is plausible but concerns an off-spec framework.

No 'realExample' or body text provides a verified language/translation/branding failure inside content[]; the only such examples are in flashcards (Nova, mythical) and the KFC anecdote, so the spec bullets most likely to appear in a 4/6-marker have the thinnest, least reliable evidence.

Difficulty ramp is flat rather than sensible: both steps are at the same descriptive level; there is no progression from definitions (approaches) to application (4Ps decisions) to strategic frameworks (Ansoff/Porter) to evaluation, even though the quiz and practice assume the last two.

content.text: Add a block on effects of change (competitiveness, productivity, financial performance, stakeholders) and key factors in successful change (organisational culture, size, speed of change, transformational leadership) plus Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies, so that quiz indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 and practice index 3 test material the lesson actually teaches; then set quizIndices/practiceIndices per block.

Fix the disruptive/step conflation: rename the type-of-change pair to incremental vs step (transformational) change across content, notes and flashcards; treat disruption as an external cause; reword the section-1 examMatters that tells firms to 'use disruptive change'.

Add recall widgets and a diagram: a reorder recall for Kotter's 8 steps (genuine procedural sequence; use one consistent wording), a fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces, and an InlineDiagram of a force field so the 'draw the diagram' advice is backed by one. Move the Toyota example to section 1 and replace the duplicate Nadella example.

Bring practice questions to IAL form: contextual 'Explain one reason... (4)' instead of 'Explain two'; convert the 6-mark Analyse to an 8-mark Assess; anchor the 10- and 20-mark stems to the bank / insurance company; replace the off-spec crisis-management question with a succession-planning or business-continuity question.

Types of Change > incremental-vs-disruptive-change > examMatters ('use disruptive change when external forces ... make the current model unsustainable'): Conflates two different concepts. The body defines disruptive change as something that 'comes from outside the established players' and 'destroys incumbents' (Christensen), i.e. a market phenomenon done TO a firm. examMatters then tells the student the firm should 'use disruptive change' as a management choice. A firm cannot 'use' disruption; it undertakes step/transformational change in response to it. The notes[] compound this with 'Disruptive (step) change' and the flashcards switch to 'transformational change', so three vocabularies for one idea.

Types of Change > drivers-and-scenario-planning > body paragraph 3, flow, keyIdea, misconception; notes[2] 'Scenario Planning': 'Scenario planning' is taught as Shell-style strategic foresight (2-4 futures, best/worst/most-likely/wildcard). In IAL 3.6.3 the heading 'Scenario planning' means identifying key risks through risk assessment (natural disasters, IT failure, loss of key staff), planning for risk mitigation (business continuity, succession planning) and the costs/benefits of contingency planning. A student who answers a 3.6.3 question with Shell scenarios will miss the indicative content entirely. The section's own quiz (Q5, Q6, Q9), flashcards (contingency, business continuity, succession, COVID) and practice Q4 use the spec meaning, so the lesson contradicts its own assessment items.

content.text: q2: Tests Kotter & Schlesinger's six strategies (education/communication, participation, facilitation, negotiation, manipulation/co-optation, coercion), which the content[] never teaches; the lesson teaches Kotter's 8-STEP model, so students will conflate the two Kotters. Answer itself (coercion) is fine as textbook framing, though K&S actually say coercion is appropriate when speed is essential.

q5: Odd wording: 'inadequate business continuity planning' is a weakness, not a risk, and 'MOST significant' is opinion with no case context. Business continuity planning is also never taught in content[] (only in flashcards). Distractors (poor marketing, excessive diversification) are nonsense for the stem.

Content/assessment mismatch is the core defect: 8 of 10 quiz MCQs (indices 0,2,3,4,5,6,7,8) and practice index 3 test spec content (Handy cultures, Kotter & Schlesinger, transformational leadership, succession planning, business continuity, size of organisation, contingency-planning costs) that the content[] blocks never teach. The PreTest draws 3 random MCQs from this bank, so most students will be pre-tested on things the lesson then ignores, and the PostTest 'improvement' is noise.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section that contains the best genuine sequence in the whole unit: Kotter's 8 steps. Also no fillin for Lewin's driving/restraining forces. Learn Mode steps therefore have no retrieval practice beyond one MCQ per block.

Zero diagrams, yet managing-change-models > examMatters instructs students to 'Draw Lewin's force field diagram'. A force field diagram (driving arrows vs restraining arrows on a line marked 'current state') is the obvious InlineDiagram and would also make the 'reduce restraining forces' insight concrete.

Only 2 blocks x 2 sections = 2 Learn Mode steps for an entire spec topic (3.6.1-3.6.3). No block covers effects of change, key factors in successful change (culture, size, speed) or risk/contingency planning. Suggested structure: Block 1 Causes and types of change; Block 2 Effects and key factors (culture, size, speed, leadership); Block 3 Managing resistance (K&S strategies + Lewin + Kotter); Block 4 Scenario/contingency planning (risk assessment, business continuity, succession, cost/benefit).

content[0] 'MNC Impact & Ethics' > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[0]: 'In extreme cases, repatriated profits exceed the original investment, making the host country a net loser.' This is a fallacy: any profitable long-lived investment eventually returns more than its initial capital; that does not make the host a net loser because the host retains wages, supplier spending, tax and capital stock. It teaches a common student error as fact.

q2: Rana Plaza appears nowhere in content[] (only flashcards[1] and common_mistakes). Because PreTest samples 3 random MCQs from this bank and InlineQuiz draws from it, students are examined on material Learn Mode never teaches.
q3: Greenwashing is not taught in content[] (flashcards only). Same untaught-material problem; and it duplicates Q9's concept, so 2 of 10 questions test one term that is not in the lesson.
q5: 'Controlling MNCs' is entirely absent from content[]. Also the stem gives the answer away: 'organisations ... campaigning' maps directly onto 'Pressure group activism'; no thinking required.

p4: 'Evaluate whether the growth of MNCs has been a positive or negative development for the global economy' — 20 marks with context: null. IAL Business 20-mark questions are always data-response, framed around a specific business/country decision in the extract ('Evaluate whether X should...' / 'Evaluate the likely impact of ... on Y'). A context-free 'global economy' essay is an Economics-style framing and cannot earn IAL application marks. Guidance is an unranked pro/con list with no levelled scheme (Level 4 = balanced, contextual judgement) and no model answer.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) and 0 diagrams: with block 1 = 2 sections and block 2 = 2 sections, the whole Learn Mode is exactly 2 steps of ~700-800 words of prose each, followed by one InlineQuiz MCQ, one practice question, ExplainItBack and a takeaway. There is no spaced/immediate recall at all, so the section is the passive-reading failure mode the founder worries about (opposite of the 'arbitrary reorder' problem).

Transfer pricing is taught twice: content[0] > mnc-negative-impacts-ethics > body[2] (full mechanism, components example) and content[1] > transfer-pricing-mechanism (full mechanism again, brand-name example, BEPS). The avoidance-vs-evasion misconception is also repeated in notes[1]. Block 2 section 2 (fdi-stakeholder-analysis) then re-sorts block 1's positives/negatives by stakeholder, so roughly half of block 2 is restatement.

No difficulty ramp and no foundation: 'FDI', 'MNC' and 'subsidiary' are used from the first sentence without definition; 'arm's length' is defined only in block 2 after transfer pricing has already been explained in block 1. All four sections sit at the same evaluative level ('net impact depends on governance') rather than definitions -> mechanisms -> evaluation.

Content[] vs assessment misalignment: quiz (6/10 items), flashcards (10/19), common_mistakes (4/6) and extras chains cover controlling MNCs, greenwashing, Rana Plaza, Nestlé, boycotts, social media — none of which appear in content[]. PreTest and InlineQuiz therefore examine students on material the lesson never presents, which is a plausible driver of pre-test demotivation.

examMatters is near-identical across all four sections (variations of 'the net impact depends on the host country's governance capacity, the MNC's industry and the regulatory framework'); the block 2 takeaway[3] repeats block 1 takeaway[2]. The evaluation template is good but repeated four times it reads as filler.

Misconceptions: 'Students assume MNCs always benefit host countries' (mnc-positive-impacts) and 'Students assume all MNCs deliberately exploit host countries' (mnc-negative-impacts-ethics) are mirror images and generic; only the avoidance/evasion and host-only-stakeholder ones are genuine, mark-scheme-relevant errors.

Block 1 title 'MNC Impact & Ethics' promises ethics, but ethics content is one sentence on labour exploitation and one on pollution havens; marketing ethics, child labour and stakeholder conflict (all spec bullets) are absent. Block 2 title 'Transfer Pricing & FDI Stakeholders' bundles two unrelated topics.

Economics framing leaks into a Business section ('current account', 'multiplier effects', 'resource curse', 'global economy' in the 20-marker); IAL Business examiners want business-decision and stakeholder framing.
Controlling MNCs: political influence, legal control, pressure groups, social media — not taught in content[] at all (only flashcards/quiz/common_mistakes)
Ethics — marketing considerations: misleading product labelling, inappropriate promotional activities (greenwashing, Nestlé formula) — absent from content[]

Ethics — stakeholder conflicts as a framing (shareholders vs workers vs communities) — implicit in fdi-stakeholder-analysis but not framed as ethical conflict
Impact on the national economy: balance of payments (export earnings vs profit repatriation and imported components) — only in flashcards[18]; content[] mentions 'current account' in one clause
Impact on the national economy: business culture — not covered anywhere
Impact on the national economy: consumers (host-country consumers: choice, price, quality) — only home-country consumers are covered

Impact on the local economy: local businesses (crowding out vs supplier opportunities) and local community and environment — covered briefly in fdi-stakeholder-analysis but not developed; wages relative to local averages (MNC wage premium) only in notes misconception

content.text: q21: correctIndex 0 ('market price exceeds its average total costs') is wrong or at best contestable. A firm continues to supply in the short run as long as price covers average VARIABLE cost (shut-down rule) and produces where P = MC; option 1 ('price is at least equal to its marginal cost') is the textbook supply condition for a price-taking firm. P > ATC is the long-run break-even condition, and a firm with P < ATC but P > AVC still supplies. This is WEC13 Unit 3 theory-of-the-firm content anyway and has no place in a WEC11 supply bank; it can be drawn into the PreTest at random.

content.text: Public Goods > characteristics-public-goods > realExample (UK lighthouse system): States lighthouses were 'historically funded by the government' and that Trinity House 'collects dues from ports rather than individual vessels'. Historically English lighthouses were largely privately built and financed by light dues levied on ships (Coase 1974 uses this as the canonical counterexample of private provision of a public good); today light dues are charged per ship tonnage on vessels calling at UK/Irish ports into the General Lighthouse Fund, not general taxation. The example undermines the point it is meant to make and is factually wrong.
content.evidence: grep -io 'lighthouse|trinity house|light dues' over the full draft bundle returns 0 hits -- the false realExample was deleted, not corrected in place (scripts/_packet25-content.mjs:43-44, 749 document the removal), so the factually-wrong claim cannot recur

content.text: Welfare Loss & Deadweight Loss > measuring-welfare-loss (body para 1): 'In a perfectly competitive market, total surplus is maximised at the equilibrium where supply meets demand. Any deviation from this point — whether through externalities, monopoly power, or government intervention — reduces total surplus.' With an externality the market equilibrium is NOT the surplus-maximising point; the externality is a property of that equilibrium, not a deviation from it, and moving away from it (a Pigouvian tax) raises welfare. This contradicts the whole Externalities block and the practice[3] model answer.
content.evidence: grep 'surplus is maximised' / 'any deviation from this point' over full bundle: 0 hits -- the 'measuring-welfare-loss' subsection no longer exists; its replacement (sub:welfare-loss-is-not-total-external-cost, scripts/_packet25-content.mjs:453) correctly states the market equilibrium is where MPB=MPC (both private curves) and the externality means that point is NOT the social optimum, never claiming the competitive equilibrium maximises total surplus under an externality

content.evidence: bundle quiz[16] 'Demand increases and the equilibrium moves from $10·600 to $12·800. Consumer surplus:' keyed (correctIndex 3) 'increases, because it is measured against the new demand curve'. Independently re-derived: Qd2 = 1400 − 50P crosses Qs = 100P − 400 at $12·800, choke $28, CS = ½·16·800 = $6,400 > $3,600. The contradicting teaching is gone: content[2].sections[3] body[2] now says 'Consumer surplus looks as though it should fall… It rises, from $3,600 to $6,400', and no string in the bundle claims CS shrinks when demand shifts.

content.text: The AD Curve > movements-along-ad > realExample: Claims 2022 UK inflation caused a movement along AD via three effects and lists 'pushed the Bank of England to raise interest rates (interest rate effect)'. The interest-rate effect behind AD's slope is the money-demand mechanism; a central bank raising the policy rate is a discretionary monetary tightening that SHIFTS AD left. The example therefore confuses the exact distinction the subsection exists to teach, and 2022 inflation was a cost-push (SRAS) episode, which the example never mentions.

content.text: Takeaways match their blocks, with one exception: content[0] takeaway 'Near full capacity the SRAS curve becomes steeper' encodes the SRAS/Keynesian-LRAS conflation noted under accuracy. Misconceptions are mostly genuine student errors (higher prices shift SRAS; government spending shifts LRAS; Keynesian AS drawn flat; equilibrium = desirable; output gap = recession); the classical-vs-keynesian-adjustment one ('Keynesians say markets never work') is a straw man rather than an observed error.
Difficulty ramp is sensible (SRAS -> LRAS -> equilibrium -> shocks -> adjustment) and pairing classical-lras with keynesian-lras in one step is the right pedagogical choice.
2.3.3 LRAS factor 'changes in relative productivity' (productivity relative to other economies) — not taught; productivity appears only as a diagram annotation and a quiz distractor.
2.3.3 LRAS factor 'demographic changes and migration' — only the word 'immigration' inside one bullet in lras-determinants; no treatment of ageing populations, participation rates or emigration.

2.3.3 LRAS factor 'changes in government regulations' — only 'deregulation' listed inside the 'Institutional factors' bullet with no explanation of the mechanism (compliance costs, labour-market rules).
2.3.3 LRAS factor 'competition policy' — named in one bullet, never explained (how contestability raises efficiency/potential output).
2.3.1 'distinction between movement along and shift of the AS curve' is taught for SRAS only; not stated for LRAS (e.g. that there is no 'movement along' a vertical LRAS).
2.5.2 (if output gaps are intended to live here) 'difficulties of measuring output gaps' — not taught; the section presents potential output as observable.

Actual vs Potential Economic Growth > actual-economic-growth > examMatters: Says to 'link actual growth to a movement along the PPF'. The guidance awards marks for the actual/potential distinction and measurement method, which a 'define' does not invite. This is also the item Learn Mode surfaces first (sortedPractice index 0, 'worked' mode) so it sets the wrong expectation.

p2: 'Assess the importance of FDI in promoting economic growth in developing countries (10 marks)' is WEC14 Unit 4 (development/FDI) content, not Unit 2 economic growth. Additionally the guidance is a points list summing to 10 (2+2+2+1+1+1+1), whereas IAL 10-mark 'Assess' is levels-marked (KAA and evaluation levels). The PPF diagram, ideal for Block 1, is never referenced by any block; Block 5 has no diagramRef at all.

Block 6 'Economic Growth and AD/AS Analysis' re-teaches Block 1 (actual = AD shift, potential = LRAS shift) and Block 4 (demand-side vs supply-side) a third time, with a duplicated reorder (potential-economic-growth vs lras-shifts-growth) and near-identical flows. 17 subsections / 11 Learn Mode steps for one spec point is long; merging Block 6 into Blocks 1 and 4 would cut ~3 steps without losing content.

Sequencing within Block 3: the four-phase overview of the cycle is introduced in the THIRD subsection ('Recovery and Stages of the Cycle', body para 2) after Boom and Recession have already been taught. The overview (and the trade-cycle diagram) should open the block.

2-per-step pairing: Block 1 = [actual, potential], [relationship]; Block 2 = [positive, negative], [implications]; Block 3 = [boom, recession], [recovery]; Block 4 = [demand, supply]; Block 5 = [benefits, env costs], [living standards]; Block 6 = [AD, LRAS], [combined]. content.text: Law of diminishing marginal productivity via marginal and average product (MP/AP curves and their link to MC/AVC) — content asserts diminishing returns raise MC but never shows product curves or a numeric example.

The IAL spec explicitly lists geographical and occupational immobility as market failure in labour markets, and the same section's own body calls discrimination 'unjustified' and immobility a 'friction' that stops differentials being competed away. A student who writes 'wage differentials are not a market failure' in an exam loses the evaluation.

Because no block has quizIndices, the legacy fallback (components/learn-mode/utils.js distributeItems) shows quiz[0], quiz[1], quiz[2] at steps 0/1/2, so this untaught question is the inline MCQ on the Trade Unions & Wage Differentials step.

The Assess (10) and Evaluate (20) questions never reach Learn Mode.

Zero recall objects across all six subsections: the spaced/immediate recall mechanism has nothing to show, so the only retrieval in the whole section is three inline MCQs. This section has several genuinely orderable chains that should be recalls (monopsony construction; NMW-in-monopsony mechanism; derived-demand chain; union wage above equilibrium → move up MRP → lower employment).

Block 2 pairing is incoherent: 'Trade Unions' is the bilateral-monopoly counterpart to monopsony and belongs with block 1; 'Wage Differentials' belongs with supply-side immobility. Suggested: Block 1 = competitive market + NMW in a competitive market; Block 2 = monopsony + trade unions/bilateral monopoly; Block 3 = wage differentials + immobility + government policy.

Firm vs market never distinguished: no subsection shows the perfectly competitive firm facing a horizontal labour supply (W = ACL = MCL) hiring where W = MRP, so the jump to 'MCL above supply' in monopsony has no baseline diagram to contrast against.

NMW in a COMPETITIVE labour market (wage floor → excess supply → unemployment) is never taught, yet monopsony-power > misconception refers to 'the standard unemployment prediction' as if it had been, and flashcard 'What is the national minimum wage' states it. The student meets the exception before the rule.

trade-unions > body flow is a list of three parallel cases (competitive / monopsony / bilateral monopoly), not a causal chain — misuse of the flow type; would confuse a reorder recall if one were later generated from it.

demand-for-labour-mrp > misconception ('firms hire workers because they need them') is filler. Real student errors here: confusing a movement along MRP (wage change) with a shift (product demand / productivity); writing MRP = MPP × price when the product market is imperfectly competitive; treating diminishing returns as workers being 'worse'.

supply-of-labour > examMatters directly contradicts the Notes-tab examMatters for the same subsection (backward-bending 'favourite diagram' vs 'most questions focus on the market supply curve'). Students switching tabs see opposite advice.
Difficulty ramp is otherwise sensible (demand/supply → competitive → monopsony → unions → differentials) and each block's takeaway list faithfully summarises its two subsections.
Elasticity of demand for labour and its determinants (labour share of cost, substitutability, PED of product, time) — not taught; tested in quiz[2].
Elasticity of supply of labour and its determinants (training period, qualifications, mobility, time) — not taught beyond one sentence.
National minimum wage in a competitive labour market (wage floor, excess supply, unemployment diagram) — only the monopsony case is covered.

Government intervention to reduce labour market failure: maximum wages, public-sector wage setting, policies to tackle geographical/occupational immobility (housing, retraining, relocation grants) — only appears in quiz[9].

Current labour market issues listed in WEC13 3.4.3 (from my recollection of the spec — treat as 'probable'): skills shortages, ageing population/retirement age, young workers, flexible/temporary/zero-hours working, migration — only migration is touched, via one flow and one misconception.

content.text: content[1] 'Competitiveness' > marshall-lerner-j-curve > realExample: Claims post-Brexit sterling depreciation produced 'a textbook J-curve' with UK exports 'gradually becoming more competitive' over two years. The UK current account deficit actually narrowed sharply in late 2016 (5.2% of GDP in 2016 to ~3.5% in 2017, driven largely by primary income valuation effects), and the widely discussed empirical finding is the absence of an export volume response (exporters raised sterling prices/margins). Presenting a contested, arguably counter-example as 'textbook' is misleading; a teacher who knows the data will object.

diagrams[0] 'Price Regulation of a Monopoly (RPI-X Price Cap)' svg: Geometry contradicts the intended teaching. The regulated price line Preg is at y=170 while the AC curve at Qreg (x=268) is at y≈115 — i.e. AC is ABOVE Preg, so the regulated firm is drawn making a loss, with no mention of this anywhere in checklist/description (the SVG comment even says 'above AC'). Also the MC=MR point is marked at (200,226) but the MC and MR paths actually intersect near (232,228), so the Qm/Pm dashed lines hang in space. The AC is U-shaped, not the falling LRAC of a natural monopoly, which is the case regulators actually price-cap.

diagrams[2] 'Effects of Privatisation and Deregulation': Represents privatisation as a rightward supply shift in a competitive S/D market ('new entry + efficiency gains'). This directly contradicts content[1] > privatisation-nationalisation body[1] ('privatising a natural monopoly simply replaces a public monopoly with a private one') and conflates privatisation with deregulation — exactly the confusion common_mistakes[1] warns against. E1 is also mis-plotted (S1 and D cross near (272,165), not (260,150)).

Obvious candidates exist: a fillin on RPI-X arithmetic; a reorder on the merger-control procedure (notification → Phase 1 → SLC test → Phase 2 → remedies/decision), which is a genuine procedural sequence; a reorder on the Averch-Johnson chain (guaranteed return on capital → incentive to over-invest → inflated capital base → productive inefficiency).

Pre-test contamination: 3 of 10 MCQs are off-topic (Q5 Laffer, Q6 occupational immobility, Q7 poverty trap); P(at least one off-topic in a 3-question pre-test) = 1 - C(7,3)/C(10,3) ≈ 71%. This is a concrete mechanism behind the founder's 'pre-test demotivates' hypothesis for this section.

Block 3 'Government Failure and Minimum Wages' pairs two unrelated topics into one step. Government failure is Unit 1 content used here as an evaluation lens (fine) and minimum wage is 3.3.4 Labour Markets content; neither is a 3.3.5 bullet. The spec's own 3.3.5 hook for labour is 'protect suppliers and employees: restricting monopsony power of firms', which is only obliquely covered.

The section is not organised around the spec's logic (why intervene → tools: mergers / monopoly control / promoting competition & contestability / protecting suppliers & employees → impacts on prices, profit, efficiency, quality, choice → limits: regulatory capture, asymmetric information). There is no summary of 'impact on prices/profit/efficiency/quality/choice' (spec 3.3.5b), so a student cannot easily answer the standard 'assess the impact of X on consumers/firms' data-response question.

Difficulty ramp is inverted: the most technical material (RPI-X vs rate-of-return, Averch-Johnson, information asymmetry) sits mid-section, while the closing block depends on 3.3.4 prerequisites (MRPL, MCL, ACL) that are assumed rather than recapped.

Takeaways match their blocks and misconceptions are genuine student errors (dominance vs abuse; RPI-X 'prices always fall'; privatisation 'always improves efficiency'; always-draw-competitive-model) — these are good. Flashcards drift off-section (consumer sovereignty, contestable market, deadweight loss, dynamic efficiency are 3.3.3), low priority.

As written it teaches the wrong comparison.

content[0] > absolute-relative-poverty > body[1], body[2], flow.steps[3], realExample ('meaning relative inequality worsened dramatically'), takeaway[1]: Relative poverty is treated as a synonym for inequality. 'Relative inequality' is not a term; a rising Gini driven by the top decile pulling away does not by itself raise relative poverty (share of households below 60% of median), which depends on the median and the bottom of the distribution. The section's own common_mistakes[0] says students must not 'confuse relative poverty with inequality', yet the body does exactly that.

q0: Answer-length cue across the bank: in 8 of 10 MCQs (indices 0,1,2,3,4,6,8,9) the correct option is the longest, usually by a wide margin. A test-wise student can score ~80% without reading the stems. Since the PreTest samples 3 of these, the pre/post-test delta is unreliable.

Only 4 subsections for a spec point with ~8 bullets; two steps total. Misconceptions: absolute-relative-poverty ('growth automatically reduces all poverty') is a real student error. lorenz-curve-gini ('Gini is a perfect measure') is filler — the real student errors are swapping the axes, reading Gini 0.4 as '40% poor', and drawing the Lorenz curve above the diagonal (common_mistakes[1] already names the axis error and should be promoted into the section). causes-inequality ('caused only by effort or talent') is ideological rather than an exam misconception. consequences-redistribution is really an evaluation point restated as a misconception.

Takeaways match their blocks (Block 1 takeaway[0-3] and Block 2 takeaway[0-3] all trace to body text). Block 2 takeaway[3] name-checks the Laffer curve, which gets one sentence in the body — thin support for a takeaway.

content[0] 'Market Failure and the State' > public-goods, merit-goods-redistribution (whole block): Public goods and merit goods are Unit 1 market-failure content (IAL 1.3.3 public goods, 1.3.4 information gaps), not 4.3.5 'Role of the state in the macroeconomy'. Presenting them as the first half of this spec point misdirects revision. Note also Edexcel IAL does not use the term 'merit good' in its spec (it uses information gaps/externalities); the term is fine as vocabulary but should not be framed as the examiner's expected answer.

p0: 'Define the term fiscal policy (4 marks)' does not match IAL command-word conventions: 'Define' is a 2-mark item; 4 marks would be 'Explain'. The guidance then awards marks for expansionary/contractionary/supply-side uses, which are not part of a definition.

Content/assessment mismatch is the defining fault: 0 of 12 MCQs, 4 of 5 practice questions, 5 of 5 diagrams and 4 of 4 extras chains cover 4.3.5 spec material that the four content[] subsections never teach; conversely nothing in quiz/practice tests public goods, merit goods, poverty traps or UBI. Pre-test (3 random MCQs) and post-test therefore measure nothing the section teaches.

Neither block has diagramRef, quizIndices or practiceIndices (content[0] and content[1] keys are only title/sections/takeaway). InlineDiagram cannot substring-match any of the 5 diagrams, so Learn Mode shows none of them; inline quiz/practice selection falls back to arbitrary items unrelated to the block just read.

Zero recall widgets (0 reorder, 0 fillin) in a section whose spec is full of genuine sequences (crowding-out chain, automatic-stabiliser chain, deficit-to-debt accumulation, transfer-pricing mechanism) and definitional contrasts ideal for fillin. Learn Mode is two text-only steps.

Block ordering/difficulty ramp: block 1 is AS-level Unit 1 content (easy, off-spec), block 2 jumps to a compressed whole-course policy overview. There is no build from 'what the state spends and taxes' through 'public finances' to 'policy in a global context', which is the spec's own ramp.

Subsection fiscal-monetary-supply-side compresses three policy tools into three paragraphs with a flow only for monetary tightening; spec 4.3.5(d) needs five tools (adds exchange rate policy, direct controls) plus TNC controls plus policymaker problems. The Agreement commits parties to hold warming 'well below 2C' and to 'pursue efforts' toward 1.5C. The $100bn/yr climate-finance pledge originated at Copenhagen (2009) and was reaffirmed in the Paris decision text, not established by the Agreement; OECD reports it was first met in 2022, so 'consistently fallen short' is dated.

content.text: 4.3.2 4b Type of trading bloc: customs unions — named but never defined or explained; a student could not answer an exam question from it. (spec-coverage audit, 12 Sep 2026)
content.evidence: content[5] > customs-unions is a full subsection: a customs union is a free-trade area plus a common external tariff, so an import pays the same duty whichever border it crosses and rules of origin between members become unnecessary; the price is that no member sets its own external tariff or signs its own trade deal. Carries a flow, a realExample, a misconception ('students say a customs union means free trade'), examMatters, and a match recall pairing each rung to the thing true only of it. Assessed by 'A free-trade area needs rules of origin because:' and 'Which policy instrument does a member give up on joining a customs union?', and by practice 'Explain the difference between a free-trade area and a customs union (4 marks)' and 'Evaluate whether a country should join a customs union (20 marks)'. A student could answer an exam question from it.

A FAILED subscription lookup now draws locks at a paying student, and packet 2.3 is what made that reachable. AuthProvider.fetchSubscription resolves .finally, so entitlementKnown becomes true even when the lookup did not answer: subscription stays null, isPremium is false, and every padlock, the upgrade CTA, the plan badge and UpgradeButton's offer draw as if the student were on the free plan. The code path is older than packet 2.3 but its REACHABILITY is not, and the verifier's note called it unchanged, which is true of only one of its two branches. On a non-ok response (res.ok false, e.g. a 500) the chain sets lookupFailed and leaves subscription ALONE - so before packet 2.3 the root layout's server seed survived and a paying student stayed premium; with the seed gone there is nothing for it to fall back to. On a network throw .catch clears subscription, which was already lossy before. Bounded: the topic-page paywall is NOT affected, because renderTab reads sectionData.isPremium from GET /api/sections/[id], an independent request with its own cookies. So the harm is cosmetic locks, the CTA bar, the plan badge and the /upgrade button, not withheld content. The ruling is the founder's and it is a values call, not a bug fix: F031 already decided in this same component that 'we could not find out' is not the same fact as 'there is no subscription' and priced it conservatively for trial eligibility (lookupFailed ? false : ...). The consistent move is to keep entitlementKnown false while lookupFailed, which tells no lie but also shows no upsell to a free student on a flaky network, possibly for the whole visit. Deliberately NOT fixed in packet 2.3: it is outside V009's acceptance checks and changes what the app says to a paying customer.

marketing.whyWrong: Nothing was retried. The number under this label is results.filter(r => !r.correct).length — the count of questions answered wrongly, each seen exactly once. The label tells the student they had a second attempt they never got.

This keeps the same number (totalRetried, i.e. questions answered incorrectly) and preserves the product's real selling point — the spaced-repetition engine schedules missed questions to come back soon (computeNextReview resets nextReview to ~10 minutes out on a wrong answer) — without asserting a retry already took place in this session. If the design wants a plainer, non-promissory label instead, "INCORRECT" (parallel to the adjacent "CORRECT" stat) is the most literal and unambiguously accurate option.

marketing.quote: MASTERED
marketing.whyWrong: A topic is badged MASTERED once 70% of its items reach repetitions >= 3, so up to 30% of the bank can be untouched. 'Mastered' itself means three correct multiple-choice answers in a bank whose options are never shuffled and where 64% of correct answers are option B, with no confidence signal collected — a student who always picks B accumulates 'mastered' items they cannot actually answer.
marketing.groundTruth: components/ProgressDashboard.jsx:63-69 (70% threshold) and app/api/progress/dashboard/route.js:69-73 (repetitions >= 3 = mastered); Finding F074 (components/practice/QuestionCard.jsx:94, severity critical) '64% of correct answers are option B; options are never shuffled anywhere'; Finding F076 (severity high) — 'a B-guesser accumulates "mastered" (repetitions>=3) cards they cannot actually answer'.
marketing.fix: Until F074 (shuffle options / rebalance correct-answer distribution) and F076 (make a real confidence signal, or an unaided second exposure, a precondition for crediting repetitions) are fixed, don't badge any topic "MASTERED." Replace the label in statusBadge() with something that describes what is actually measured, not an outcome the data can't support: swap 'MASTERED' for 'ON TRACK' (or 'STRONG PROGRESS' if width allows), keep the same >=70% threshold and green color so the motivational/reward intent is preserved, and add a tooltip/subtext on the badge or ring: '70%+ answered correctly 3x in spaced review' so the claim is scoped to the actual mechanism instead of implying verified subject mastery. Reintroduce 'MASTERED' as copy only after the option-shuffle and confidence-gating fixes land, since at that point the underlying metric will actually support the word.
